analysis.investment_thesis: Cemindia Projects trades at a P/B of 5.44 — nearly four times my upper tolerance — and its computed Graham Number of approximately INR 241 implies the current price of INR 648 carries a 169% premium to intrinsic value. A construction and civil engineering contractor with a history of losses and thin margins should never command such a multiple.
key_strengths: Strong revenue acceleration: INR 3,809 Cr in FY22 to INR 9,097 Cr in FY25 — India's infrastructure boom is a genuine tailwind
Debt/Equity of 0.48 is marginally within my 0.5 ceiling — the balance sheet is not dangerously leveraged
ROCE of 27.6% and ROE of 21.8% show improving capital efficiency in recent years
key_risks: Net profit was negative (loss of INR 59 Cr) in FY15 and nearly negligible at INR 16 Cr in FY21 — the earnings record does not meet my requirement of 5+ consecutive years of positive profits
Operating margin of only 7.74% in construction offers almost no cushion against project cost overruns, material inflation, or payment delays from government clients
Recent ownership change (subsidiary of Renew Exim DMCC as of August 2025) and company name change introduce governance uncertainty I cannot adequately price
red_flags: P/B of 5.44 is more than 3.6x my maximum threshold of 1.5 — paying INR 5.44 for every rupee of book value in a cyclical, capital-intensive industry is speculation, not investment
Earnings history is discontinuous (data gap in 2018) and included losses and near-zero profits as recently as FY21
Free cash flow collapsed to INR 30 Cr in FY25 from INR 369 Cr in FY24 despite surging revenue — working capital absorption in construction is a perennial trap
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The construction and civil engineering sector is inherently project-based, meaning revenues and profits lurch from year to year depending on contract awards, execution pace, and client payment behavior. I require a business with a long, unbroken record of profitability precisely because I wish to base valuation on demonstrated, not hoped-for, earning power. Cemindia's history of a net loss in FY15, trivial profits in FY20–21, and significant data gaps is the antithesis of the stability I demand.

The valuation of INR 648 per share — a 169% premium to the Graham Number — reflects the market's enthusiasm for India's infrastructure capex cycle, not the company's proven intrinsic worth. Market enthusiasm is exactly when I become most skeptical. I require a margin of safety; Mr. Market is offering a margin of danger. I would require the price to fall to near book value before considering this company further.
